ex: She won the 100-meter sprint at the school competition.
He finished the race with a fast sprint at the end.
The runners train for the sprint every morning.
I made a short sprint to catch the bus.

tonic.note: Often called "tonic water." A drink with it: "a gin and tonic."

bureaucrat.note: Often negative: an official who cares too much about rules and forms.

recruiting.note: Uncountable. Most often a verb form: "The company is recruiting new staff."
ex: She works in recruiting at a big tech company.
Our recruiting team reads hundreds of resumes every week.
Online recruiting helps companies find workers faster.
He wants a job in recruiting after college.

nationalism.note: Uncountable: no "a" and usually no plural.

ex: This photo is 1,000 pixels wide and 600 pixels tall.
Zoom in and you can see each pixel.
This new screen has more pixels than my old one.
One pixel on my monitor is always black.

ambassador.note: Most often "ambassador" is a top diplomat: "the US ambassador to Ukraine." Here: a brand ambassador.

bailiff.note: In the US, a court officer who keeps order; in the UK, also someone who takes things for unpaid debts.

ogre.note: Also used for a cruel, scary person: "My boss is an ogre."
ex: In the fairy tale, an ogre lives under the bridge.
The ogre in the story was big, green, and grumpy.
The children ran away from the hungry ogre.
My son wore an ogre costume to the party.

suspense.note: Uncountable. Common phrase: "keep someone in suspense."
ex: The movie kept me in suspense until the very end.
I love books with a lot of suspense.
Please tell us the news and don't keep us in suspense.
The suspense in the last scene was too much for me.

cube.note: Often a small block: "an ice cube," "a sugar cube." In math: "the cube of 2 is 8."

ex: The police arrested two extremists near the airport.
He was arrested as a dangerous political extremist.
Extremists often spread hate and fear online.
The group was led by a religious extremist.

bloc.note: A group of countries or parties that work together. Not the same as "block."

ex: The city holds an LGBT pride parade every June.

nomad.note: "Digital nomad": a person who works online while traveling.
ex: The nomads moved their tents with the seasons.

Desert nomads often travel with camels and goats.
Digital nomads work from cafes in different countries.
Good storytelling keeps people listening until the end.
She teaches storytelling to kids at the library.
Storytelling is an important skill in marketing and sales.
The movie is a great example of visual storytelling.

caesar.note: Most often "Caesar" is the name of Julius Caesar, or a "Caesar salad." Usually capitalized.
ex: In ancient Rome, each new emperor took the title Caesar.
The Roman Senate was afraid of the new Caesar.
Coins from that time show the face of the Caesar.
The Caesar ruled a huge empire from Rome.

Buddhist.note: Most often an adjective: "a Buddhist temple." Always capitalized.
ex: He is a Buddhist and meditates every morning.
Buddhists celebrate this holiday in the spring.
She became a Buddhist after a long trip to Asia.
Many Buddhists do not eat meat.

hospice.note: In the US, also the care itself: "She is in hospice."

ex: She has a calm temperament and rarely gets angry.
This dog breed has a gentle temperament.
His patient temperament makes him a good teacher.
The two sisters have very different temperaments.

crossword.note: We say "do a crossword." Also "crossword puzzle."

pretext.note: Common: "on/under the pretext of," "a pretext for."

ex: The boss gave him an ultimatum: work harder or leave.
The government ignored the ultimatum from the workers.
She gave her boyfriend an ultimatum about his smoking.
The ultimatum ends at midnight on Friday.

c'est la vie.note: French for "that's life"; said when something bad happens that you cannot change.
ex: We missed the last train home, but c'est la vie.
It rained all week on our vacation, but c'est la vie.
I didn't get the job, but c'est la vie.
My phone broke again. C'est la vie, I guess.

cache.note: Pronounced like "cash." Also a hidden store: "a cache of weapons."

ex: She gave a talk at a medical symposium last month.
The university hosts a symposium on climate change every year.
Experts from many countries attended the symposium.
The symposium will last three days.
Can you add some mayonnaise to my sandwich?
I don't like mayonnaise on my fries.
Mix the tuna with a spoon of mayonnaise.
The jar of mayonnaise is in the fridge.

micro.note: Usually used as a prefix: microchip, microwave.

lasagna.note: Usually uncountable: some lasagna. British spelling: "lasagne."
ex: My mom makes lasagna for dinner every Sunday.
This lasagna has three kinds of cheese.
Heat the lasagna in the oven for twenty minutes.
Can I have another piece of lasagna, please?

The old roof is made of zinc.
Nuts, meat, and beans contain a lot of zinc.
Zinc is used to protect steel from rust.

charisma.note: Uncountable: a lot of charisma (not "a charisma").

icing.note: Uncountable. In American English, "frosting" is more common for soft cake icing.

vocalist.note: "Singer" is more common in everyday speech.

omega.note: Often in "omega-3" (healthy fats in fish) and "alpha and omega" (the beginning and the end).

vandalism.note: Uncountable: an act of vandalism (not "a vandalism").

The police arrested two teenagers for vandalism.
New cameras helped reduce vandalism downtown.
